teach.what: A mudslide buried a sea floor so fast that soft bodies, including legs, guts, and eyes, turned to stone. The fossil is Anomalocaris, a top predator. The drawing is five-eyed Opabinia, a different animal from these rocks.
teach.when: About 508 million years ago, in the Middle Cambrian, when animals were brand-new.
teach.where: High in the Rocky Mountains of Yoho National Park, British Columbia, Canada.
teach.why: It is one of the best snapshots of the Cambrian explosion, when most animal body plans first appeared.

UNESCO World Heritage: Canadian Rocky Mountain Parks (includes the Burgess Shale)

teach.what: Animals that sank into a deep volcanic lake were preserved whole, with skin, feathers, fur outlines, and even last meals. The fossil is Darwinius, nicknamed Ida. The model is Propalaeotherium, an early horse from the same pit, not the same animal.
teach.when: About 48 million years ago, in the Middle Eocene.
teach.where: The Messel Pit, near Frankfurt in Hesse, Germany.
teach.why: It shows the early days of modern mammals after the dinosaurs, including tiny early horses and some of the first bats. More than 1,000 species of plants and animals have been found here.

teach.what: Rivers buried dinosaurs in sand and mud on a warm coastal plain. Wind and rain now uncover them in the badlands. The skeleton is Gorgosaurus, a tyrannosaur. The drawing is Centrosaurus, a horned dinosaur. They are different animals from this park.
teach.when: 75 to 77 million years ago, in the Late Cretaceous.
teach.why: More than 44 dinosaur species and more than 350 articulated skeletons have been found here. It is one of the richest places to see who lived together in the last chapter of the dinosaurs.

sites.n: La Brea Tar Pits, Los Angeles, USA

teach.what: Sticky asphalt trapped Ice Age animals and preserved their bones, including saber-toothed cats, dire wolves, mammoths, and giant ground sloths. Both pictures are a saber-toothed cat (Smilodon).
teach.when: The last ice age, from about 50,000 to 10,000 years ago.
teach.where: The La Brea Tar Pits, in Los Angeles, California, USA.
teach.why: It is the world’s richest Ice Age fossil site in a city. Scientists still dig here in public view, and the bones show how animals and climate changed as people arrived.

restoration.credit: Charles Robert Knight, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. Artist’s illustration.
restoration.caption: Saber-toothed cat (Smilodon)

teach.what: Before animals had shells, bones, or legs, the sea floor was covered in soft creatures shaped like discs, fronds, and ribbons. The fossil is Dickinsonia costata, from these hills. The drawing is Dickinsonia menneri, a related species.
teach.when: About 560 to 542 million years ago, in the Ediacaran Period. Reg Sprigg found the imprints here in 1946, and that age is named after these hills.
teach.where: The Ediacara Hills in the Flinders Ranges, at Nilpena Ediacara National Park, South Australia.
teach.why: It is the dawn of animal life. Dickinsonia is among the oldest known animals, and tiny Ikaria may be an early ancestor of animals with a left and right side, like us. The Flinders Ranges are on UNESCO’s Tentative List (a nomination was submitted in 2026). They are not a World Heritage site yet.

learnMore.label: UNESCO Tentative List: Flinders Ranges (not inscribed yet)

restoration.caption: Dickinsonia menneri

teach.what: Whole skeletons of early whales, still with tiny back legs and feet. The photo is a Basilosaurus isis jaw in the rock. The drawing is Basilosaurus cetoides, a related species.
teach.when: About 40 to 37 million years ago, in the Late Eocene.
teach.where: Wadi Al-Hitan, Whale Valley, in the Fayoum, Egypt. This desert was a shallow sea then.
teach.why: Whales used to walk. This is the most important place to see them changing from land animals into ocean swimmers. The rocks also hold Dorudon.

restoration.caption: Basilosaurus cetoides

teach.what: These rocks record the Triassic, when the first dinosaurs and the first mammal relatives appeared. The pictures are Eoraptor, a small early meat-eater. The skull is a museum cast, not the original fossil.
teach.when: About 231 to 225 million years ago, in the Late Triassic. The valley’s rocks span much of the Triassic, about 250 to 200 million years ago.
teach.where: Ischigualasto Provincial Park, the Valley of the Moon, in San Juan, Argentina.
teach.why: It is the opening scene of the Age of Dinosaurs. Early meat-eaters such as Eoraptor and Herrerasaurus were found here.

teach.what: Sea reptiles, fish, ammonites, and shrimp-like animals sank into a calm tropical lagoon. The pictures are Tanystropheus, a reptile with a neck longer than its body.
teach.when: 245 to 230 million years ago, in the Middle Triassic.
teach.where: Monte San Giorgio, by Lake Lugano, on the border of Ticino, Switzerland, and Lombardy, Italy.
teach.why: It is the best-known record of ocean life from the Triassic, just after Earth’s biggest mass extinction.

restoration.credit: Nobu Tamura, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Artist’s illustration.

teach.what: Some of the oldest large, complex animal-like life ever found. These are soft, frond-shaped seafloor creatures pressed into rock.
teach.when: 580–560 million years ago, in the Ediacaran Period, before animals had shells or bones.
teach.where: Sea cliffs at Mistaken Point, on Newfoundland’s southeastern tip, Canada.
teach.why: It shows life getting big for the first time, in a deep ocean. Volcanic ash buried the seafloor and kept the shapes.

teach.what: Animals preserved in amazing detail, sometimes including soft body parts. The pictures are Fuxianhuia protensa, an arthropod from this site.
teach.when: About 530 million years ago, during the Cambrian explosion.
teach.why: Almost all of today’s major animal groups got their start in this short burst of time.

sites.n: Joggins Fossil Cliffs, Nova Scotia, Canada

teach.what: Whole fossil trees still stand upright in the cliffs, and some of the earliest reptiles were preserved inside hollow trunks.
teach.when: The Coal Age (Carboniferous), about 300 million years ago. UNESCO dates these rock layers to 318–303 million years ago.
teach.where: The Bay of Fundy shore at Joggins, Nova Scotia, Canada.
teach.why: Swamp forests like these became much of the world’s coal, which ties this cliff to the climate story. UNESCO and Parks Canada call the reptiles here the earliest amniotes in these rocks.

sites.n: Petrified Forest National Park, Arizona, USA

teach.what: Logs that slowly turned into colorful stone (quartz), along with early dinosaurs and their relatives. The drawing is Chindesaurus, an early dinosaur found in this park.
teach.when: Late Triassic, more than 200 million years ago.
teach.where: Petrified Forest National Park, Arizona, USA.
teach.why: It records life on land after the greatest extinction of all time, when forests and early dinosaurs shared a river plain.

teach.what: A rock wall in the Quarry Exhibit Hall still holds about 1,500 dinosaur bones. The National Park Service names Allosaurus, Apatosaurus, Camarasaurus, Diplodocus, and Stegosaurus among them.
teach.when: Late Jurassic, about 150 million years ago.
teach.where: Dinosaur National Monument, on the Utah–Colorado border, USA.
teach.why: It shows an ancient river ecosystem and how the animals were buried together in the Morrison Formation.

teach.what: 155 km of coastline whose rock layers hold about 185 million years of Earth history, including marine reptiles such as Ichthyosaurus from Lyme Regis.
teach.when: Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous time, stacked in one coast.
teach.where: The Dorset and East Devon coast, England.
teach.why: The coast keeps eroding, so new fossils keep appearing. People have studied these cliffs for over 300 years.

teach.what: Fossils of ancient marsupials. The pictures are Nimbadon lavarackorum, a wombat relative from Riversleigh. Naracoorte’s caves also hold ice-age animals, including the marsupial lion.
teach.when: The last tens of millions of years. Riversleigh’s mammals are about 30 to 10 million years old. Naracoorte records a later ice age.
teach.where: Riversleigh in Queensland and Naracoorte in South Australia. This pin sits at Riversleigh.
teach.why: Australia was almost on its own for about 35 million years after it split from Antarctica, so its mammals became unique as habitats changed.

teach.what: Caves full of fossils of early human relatives, including the Taung Child, a young Australopithecus africanus.
teach.when: From more than 3.5 million years ago up toward the recent past.
teach.where: Sterkfontein, Swartkrans, Kromdraai, the Makapan Valley, and Taung, South Africa.
teach.why: It is a main record of how our own family tree changed across more than 3.5 million years.
